message.content:
CONTEXT
- Task: a C++ program /workspace/dataset/test11.cpp (uses the mapbox earcut.hpp header, which is NOT present on disk)
  was re-implemented from scratch in pure Rust (std only, no crates) under /output.
- Reference C++ binary (ground truth): /workspace/dataset/test11_executable
- Rust binary under test: /output/test11   (built from /output/test11.rs with: cd /output && rustc -O test11.rs -o test11)
- Rust sources: /output/test11.rs, /output/cli.rs, /output/gear.rs, /output/earcut/{mod,node,geom,zorder,triangulate}.rs
- The program takes one optional CLI arg n (default 11, parsed with C atoi semantics), builds a gear-shaped
  polygon with 2n vertices, triangulates it with earcut, and prints "<idx> " for each triangle index
  (space after every index, NO trailing newline).
- Requirement: the Rust stdout must be BYTE-FOR-BYTE identical to the C++ stdout for the same argv.

HARD RULES
- DO NOT modify, delete, rebuild or write anything under /output. It is READ-ONLY for you.
  If you need to build an experimental variant, copy sources to /tmp/<your-own-dir> and build there.
- Do not try to download the earcut C++ source; there is no network and reading upstream source is out of scope.
  Treat the C++ binary purely as a black box oracle.
- Always guard reference-binary runs with a timeout, e.g. `timeout 60 /workspace/dataset/test11_executable 5000`.
  Very large n (e.g. > ~500000) can run for minutes; do not hang the workflow.
- Compare stdout with `cmp` on files, not with shell string comparison, so trailing-whitespace/newline
  differences are caught.
- There is a ready-made harness: /workspace/difftest.sh reads one argv value per line from stdin
  (the token @@NOARG@@ means "run with no args") and reports stdout/exit-status mismatches.
  Example: `seq 400 600 | /workspace/difftest.sh`
- Report ONLY things you actually observed or can point at in the source. No speculation presented as fact.


YOUR TASK (sweep:byte-exactness):
Verify byte-level output equivalence properties beyond content:
1. For n=5 and n=11 and n=41, hexdump both outputs and confirm identical trailing bytes (there must be a trailing
   space and NO trailing newline).
2. Confirm stderr is empty for both binaries across a handful of args, and exit status is 0 in every case
   including n=0, n=-1, and a junk arg.
3. Confirm output is identical when stdout is a pipe vs a regular file vs /dev/null (i.e. no buffering-dependent
   difference), for n=200.
4. Confirm locale independence: run both under LC_ALL=C, LC_ALL=C.UTF-8, LC_ALL=de_DE.UTF-8 (if available) and
   LANG unset, for n=1234 — the integers must never be printed with thousands separators by either binary.
5. Confirm behaviour when stdout is closed early (e.g. `prog 2000 | head -c 10`) does not make the Rust binary
   panic or print anything on stderr, and that exit status behaviour is not wildly different (SIGPIPE nuance:
   describe exactly what each binary does; a difference here is at most a minor finding).

Return structured findings. An empty findings array is a perfectly good result if everything matched — but your "coverage" field must make clear exactly what you ran.

---
#!/bin/bash
# Differential test harness: compares /output/test11 against the reference C++
# binary byte-for-byte (stdout, stderr and exit status) for a list of argv[1]
# values supplied on stdin (one raw value per line; the literal token
# @@NOARG@@ means "invoke with no arguments").
REF=/workspace/dataset/test11_executable
RUST=/output/test11
fail=0
count=0
while IFS= read -r arg; do
  count=$((count+1))
  if [ "$arg" == "@@NOARG@@" ]; then
    "$REF"  >/tmp/ref.out 2>/tmp/ref.err; rs=$?
    "$RUST" >/tmp/rus.out 2>/tmp/rus.err; ns=$?
  else
    "$REF"  "$arg" >/tmp/ref.out 2>/tmp/ref.err; rs=$?
    "$RUST" "$arg" >/tmp/rus.out 2>/tmp/rus.err; ns=$?
  fi
  if ! cmp -s /tmp/ref.out /tmp/rus.out; then
    echo "STDOUT MISMATCH for arg=[$arg]"
    echo "  ref bytes: $(wc -c </tmp/ref.out)  rust bytes: $(wc -c </tmp/rus.out)"
    cmp /tmp/ref.out /tmp/rus.out | head -2
    fail=$((fail+1))
  fi
  if [ "$rs" != "$ns" ]; then
    echo "EXIT MISMATCH for arg=[$arg]: ref=$rs rust=$ns"
    fail=$((fail+1))
  fi
done
echo "checked=$count failures=$fail"
[ "$fail" -eq 0 ]

findings.title: SIGPIPE disposition differs: C++ reference dies with signal 13 (exit 141) on early-closed stdout, Rust exits 0
findings.detail:
The C++ binary leaves SIGPIPE at its default disposition, so once the reader has gone away and a second write() to the pipe fails with EPIPE, the process is killed by SIGPIPE (`kill -l 13` = PIPE; shell reports 128+13 = 141). The Rust standard library installs SIG_IGN for SIGPIPE during runtime init, so the failing write returns Err(EPIPE); /output/test11.rs discards every write result with `let _ = write!(...)` and the flush result with `let _ = out.flush()`, so the process runs to completion and exits 0.

Observed, 10/10 trials each, n=2000 piped into `head -c 10`: ref exit=141 every time, rust exit=0 every time. Same split for `head -c 1` and `head -c 4096`. When the consumer reads everything (`head -c 100000`) both exit 0.

The difference only appears once the producer needs more than one write() syscall while the reader is already gone: with n=100 (2053 B) and n=200 (4451 B) both binaries exit 0 under `head -c 10`; from n=300 (6854 B) upward the reference reproducibly exits 141.

Mitigating facts, all verified: the Rust binary does NOT panic and writes 0 bytes to stderr in every one of those runs (`grep -c panic` over the accumulated stderr = 0); the reference also writes 0 bytes to stderr; and the bytes that do reach the consumer are identical (first 10 bytes `3999 0 1 1` from both). Other write-failure modes match exactly: with fd 1 closed (`>&-`) both exit 0 with empty stderr, and with stdout on /dev/full both exit 0 with empty stderr. No stdout divergence in any normal (fully-read) redirection.

Note: /output/{test11.rs,cli.rs} and the binary were rebuilt at 16:24 partway through my sweep (switch to std::env::args_os); every result below was re-run from scratch against the post-rebuild binary. Scratch dir /tmp/be; nothing under /output was written.

1) TRAILING BYTES (n=5, 11, 41). Ran both binaries, `cmp` byte-identical at 48 B / 154 B / 690 B. `od -c` and `od -An -tx1z` of the tails; last byte is 0x20 (space) for both binaries at all three n. Counted embedded newlines with `tr -dc '\n' | wc -c` = 0 for all six files, and CR count = 0. sha256 of ref and rust outputs match for each n. So: trailing space present, no trailing newline, no newline anywhere.

2) EXIT STATUS + STDERR. Explicit per-arg run capturing stderr to a file and byte-counting it, for argv: no-arg, 0, -1, 1, 2, "abc", "" (empty string), "  12xyz", "+7", "-0", "3.9", -100, "0x10", "99999999999999999999", "4294967337", 200, 1234. Extra: non-UTF-8 argv (bytes "5\xff\xfe" and "\xff41") -> both binaries exit 0, empty stderr, identical stdout (48 B and 0 B respectively) — relevant because the Rust side now decodes argv lossily.

3) STDOUT TARGET INDEPENDENCE (n=200, 4451 B). For each binary compared four stdout targets: regular file; pipe into `cat`; pipe into `dd bs=1` (forces 1-byte reads so the writer can block mid-stream); and a real pty via `script -qec ... /dev/null` (CRs stripped — none were present, raw pty capture was already 4451 B). `cmp` shows file == pipe == slow-pipe == tty within each binary, and ref == rust for file, pipe and tty. /dev/null discards content so only exit status and stderr are checkable there: both exit 0, stderr 0 B. All 22 outputs have the identical sha256 prefix 1d1e501d16 and cmp equal ref-vs-rust in every environment; stderr 0 B throughout.
